https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Angle relationships
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: A linear pair measures 4x + 5 and 3x degrees. Find x and both angles. Explain why addition, rather than equality, is appropriate.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: 7x + 5 = 180 gives x = 25. The angles are 105° and 75°. They are supplementary, not necessarily congruent.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Parallel lines and transversals
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: A transversal cuts parallel lines. One angle is 64°. Find its corresponding angle and its adjacent linear-pair angle. State each reason.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: The corresponding angle is 64° by the parallel-lines theorem. The adjacent angle is 116° because a linear pair sums to 180°.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Proof and counterexamples
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Evaluate: 'If two angles are congruent, they are vertical angles.' Give a counterexample and identify the true related theorem.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: Two separate right angles are congruent but need not be opposite angles at an intersection. Vertical angles are congruent; the converse is false.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Triangle angle sums
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: A triangle has angles x, 2x, and 3x degrees. Find the angles and the exterior angle at the largest angle.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: 6x = 180, so x = 30. The angles are 30°, 60°, 90°. The exterior angle adjacent to 90° is 90°.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Congruence criteria
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Two triangles have angle measures 40°, 60°, and 80°. Must they be congruent? Describe a construction that tests your claim.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: No. Enlarge one triangle by scale factor 2. Its angles stay equal while its side lengths double. AAA establishes similarity, not congruence.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Isosceles triangles and midsegments
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: An isosceles triangle has base angles of 72°. Find its vertex angle. A midsegment parallel to its base is 9 cm; find the base.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: The vertex angle is 180 − 144 = 36°. The base is twice the midsegment, so it measures 18 cm.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Scale factors and similarity
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Two similar rectangles have corresponding widths 4 and 10. If the smaller area is 24 square units, find the larger area and explain the exponent.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: The length factor is 10/4 = 2.5. Area uses two dimensions, so its factor is 2.5² = 6.25. The larger area is 150 square units.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: The Pythagorean theorem
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: A ladder 13 ft long reaches a wall while its base is 5 ft from the wall. Assuming a right angle at the ground, how high does it reach?
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: The ladder is the hypotenuse. Height² = 13² − 5² = 144, so height = 12 ft. Adding the squares would incorrectly treat a leg as the hypotenuse.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Right-triangle trigonometry
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: For the other acute angle of the same 3–4–5 triangle, give sine, cosine, and tangent. Explain what swaps.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: Sine = 4/5, cosine = 3/5, tangent = 4/3. Opposite and adjacent swap when the reference angle changes; the hypotenuse remains 5.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Arcs and circle angles
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: An inscribed angle measures 57°. Find its intercepted arc and a central angle intercepting that same arc.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: The intercepted arc is 114°. The central angle is also 114°. Doubling applies to the inscribed angle, not to an already-central angle.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Circle length and area
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: A circle has diameter 10 cm. Find the circumference and the area of a 90° sector.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: The radius is 5 cm. Circumference = 10π cm. The sector area is (1/4)(25π) = 25π/4 cm².

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Distance, midpoint, and circles
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Find the center and radius of (x + 3)² + (y − 2)² = 49. Test whether (4,2) lies on it.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: The center is (−3,2), the radius is 7. Substitution gives 7² + 0² = 49, so (4,2) lies on the circle.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Area by decomposition
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: A parallelogram has base 12, perpendicular height 5, and slanted side 7. Find its area and perimeter, explaining why different measurements are used.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: Area = 12×5 = 60 square units. Perimeter = 2(12 + 7) = 38 units. Height measures separation between parallel bases, not boundary length.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Volumes and surface areas
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Compare a cone and cylinder with radius 4 and height 9. Find each volume, with units.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: Cylinder volume = π(4²)(9) = 144π cubic units. Cone volume = (1/3)(144π) = 48π cubic units. The one-third relation assumes equal base areas and heights.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.title: Rigid motions and symmetry
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Translate (−1,4) by (3,−2), then reflect across the y-axis. Give both intermediate and final points and identify what remains invariant.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/geo.selfCheck: Translation gives (2,2); reflection gives (−2,2). Distances and angles are preserved by both transformations, although orientation reverses under reflection.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Evaluate 17 / 5, 17 % 5, and (double)17 / 5. Explain why the three results differ.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: The texts are "5 points" and "points 23". Use first.equals(second) when first is non-null, or a null-safe equality helper.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: Boolean expressions
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: For a = true and b = false, evaluate !(a && b) and !a && !b. Are they equivalent for all inputs?
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: The first is true; the second is false. They are not equivalent. De Morgan's law gives !(a && b) equivalent to !a || !b.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: Selection and boundary cases
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Design a mutually exclusive condition chain for negative, zero, and positive integers. Show which branch handles −1, 0, and 1.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: Use if (n < 0), else if (n == 0), else. The three cases are disjoint and cover every int. Values −1, 0, and 1 exercise all branches.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: Tracing nested conditions
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Trace the same code when x = −1 and y = 8. Which comparisons execute, and which variables change?
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: Only x > 0 executes, and it is false. The entire inner block is skipped. x stays −1 and y stays 8.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: Count-controlled loops
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: How many times does for (int i = 2; i <= 10; i += 2) execute? List every value of i used in its body.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: It executes five times, using 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10. The next update gives 12, which fails the condition.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: Accumulators and invariants
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Trace int product = 1; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) product *= i;. Explain what would happen if product began at zero.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: The partial products are 1, 2, 6, 24. Starting at zero keeps every product zero, so the multiplicative identity must be 1.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: While loops and termination
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Trace int n = 3; int count = 0; while (n < 20) { n *= 2; count++; }. Give final values and a termination argument.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: n takes 6, 12, and 24; count ends at 3. Doubling a positive integer eventually crosses this finite threshold, with these small values avoiding overflow.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: Methods and parameters
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: For static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }, trace int x = 3; int z = add(x, x + 1);. What are x and z?
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: Arguments evaluate to 3 and 4; the method returns 7. x remains 3 because the method receives values, not a writable alias to the caller's local variable.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: Classes and encapsulation
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: A BankAccount stores a nonnegative balance. What must a withdrawal method check before subtracting an amount? Include a negative-amount case.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: It must reject negative withdrawals and withdrawals exceeding the balance. Otherwise subtracting a negative amount could improperly increase the balance, or excessive withdrawal could break the invariant.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: References and aliases
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Create a reference diagram for Counter a = new Counter(); Counter b = a; b = new Counter();. How many objects exist, and are a and b aliases at the end?
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: Two Counter objects were created. Initially a and b were aliases; after b's reassignment they refer to different objects.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: Array indices and traversal
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Trace int[] a = {1, 3, 5}; for (int v : a) { v *= 2; }. What does a contain afterward, and how would you actually double its elements?
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: a still contains 1, 3, 5. Use for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] *= 2; to replace each element.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: Searching and edge cases
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: Write pseudocode to return the first index of target in an array, or −1. Explain its worst-case number of element comparisons for length n.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: Visit indices 0 through n−1; return i when values[i] equals target; return −1 after the loop. The worst case uses n comparisons when the match is last or absent.

https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.title: Nested loops and complexity
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.license: Original lesson; linked reference is not reproduced
recallPrompts: For n = 4, count executions when i ranges 0..<n and j ranges 0..<i. List the count contributed by each outer iteration.
https://firststatelens.local/lessons/pre.selfCheck: The contributions are 0, 1, 2, and 3, totaling 6 = n(n−1)/2. The bound grows quadratically even though fewer than n² bodies execute.
